name: Peripheral nerve injury (Seddon/Sunderland)
populations: people with high-energy trauma, fractures or dislocations
athletes with severe ligament or multiligament knee injuries
people with lacerations or penetrating injuries
people with sustained or repeated pressure over a nerve at a tunnel or bony prominence
summary: Injury to a peripheral nerve, graded by Seddon (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis) and Sunderland. Recovery depends on the grade and is slow at about 1 mm a day; no sign of recovery means early referral.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Neurapraxia is presumed to recover within about 8–12 weeks; after axonal injury, axons regrow at about 1 mm a day, so recovery takes months and depends on the distance to the target muscle

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. Protect the denervated limb, track reinnervation, and rebuild strength as muscles recover; return depends on grade, site and muscle recovery

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Motor and sensory loss in one nerve's territory with a typical mechanism; document a baseline and repeat serially, with an advancing Tinel sign as a clinical sign of regrowth

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Electrodiagnostic study (nerve conduction and EMG) localises and grades the injury; useful information can be obtained in the first week, though it is conventionally delayed to about 3 weeks

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No general incidence figure was identified in the abstracts reviewed; the common peroneal nerve is injured in 16% to 40% of multiligament knee injuries

keyFacts.label: Early referral
keyFacts.value: Refer when there is no clinical or electrical sign of recovery, with an open wound or progressive deficit, or with a proximal injury, where decisions must be made more quickly

overview:
Traumatic peripheral nerve injury (TPNI) commonly results from penetrating injury, crush, stretch or ischaemia [r1]. Severity is classified as neurapraxia, axonotmesis or neurotmesis in Seddon's classification, or into five degrees in Sunderland's classification [r2,r3]. Neurapraxia is a conduction block with the axon intact; axonotmesis disrupts the axon with Wallerian degeneration of the part beyond the lesion; neurotmesis is complete transection and usually needs surgical repair [r2,r1]. Much is known about the mechanisms of injury and regeneration, yet reliable treatments that ensure full functional recovery are scarce [r4].

The physiotherapist's role is to recognise a nerve injury, record a careful baseline, protect the limb, maintain joint range and muscle health during the long wait for regrowth, and make sure that a child, athlete or older adult who is not recovering reaches a surgeon in time. Decisions about whether and when to operate depend on the injury, and proximal injuries need quicker decisions because the long distance makes it difficult to reinnervate distal muscles before irreversible changes occur [r1]. Evidence for exercise and electrical stimulation during regeneration is mostly preclinical and human data are scarce [r5].

epidemiology.text: No general population incidence for peripheral nerve injury was identified in the abstracts reviewed, so none is quoted; epidemiology and classification of traumatic nerve injuries are reviewed by Robinson [r6]. In sport and orthopaedic trauma, high-risk settings can be identified. The common peroneal nerve (CPN) is injured in 16% to 40% of multiligament knee injuries, which are themselves uncommon (under 0.02% of all orthopaedic injuries), and CPN injuries have a poor prognosis compared with other peripheral nerve injuries [r7]. Traumatic brachial plexus injuries are devastating, with effects on physical, psychosocial, mental and financial well-being [r8]. Common acute causes are penetrating injury, crush, stretch and ischaemia [r1].

intrinsic: A superficial course next to bone, such as the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck, which is predisposed to injury during local trauma and dislocation [r7]
Passage through a fibro-osseous tunnel, where limited space makes the nerve vulnerable to compression (anatomical reasoning)
Proximal injuries carry a worse functional outlook because of the long distance to the target muscles [r1]
Age and general health, and conditions such as diabetes that reduce nerve resilience (clinical reasoning; not quantified in the sources read)
extrinsic: Penetrating injury (laceration), crush, stretch and ischaemia [r1]
Severe ligament injury and joint dislocation, particularly a varus stress with posterolateral corner injury at the knee [r7]
Fractures and high-energy trauma, including gunshot or other multi-tissue injuries (clinical reasoning)
Prolonged or repeated external pressure, such as a tight cast, strap or sustained position (clinical reasoning)

mechanism.summary: Nerves are injured by cutting, crushing, stretching or by ischaemia [r1]. In sport and trauma the commonest mechanisms are a direct blow or sustained pressure that compresses the nerve against bone or in a tight tunnel, and traction when a joint is forced beyond its range, as when varus stress at the knee stretches the common peroneal nerve around the fibular neck [r7,r1]. Mild compression blocks conduction without destroying the axon (neurapraxia). Greater force or longer duration disrupts axons, causing Wallerian degeneration beyond the lesion, and complete disruption leaves a gap that does not recover without surgery [r1,r2].
sequence: A force acts on the nerve: a blow, sustained pressure, a stretch or a laceration [r1].
The nerve is compressed against bone or in a tight tunnel, or stretched across a joint forced beyond its range [r7].
Local blood flow to the nerve is reduced and the nerve fibres lose conduction at the injury site (mechanistic model).
In neurapraxia, conduction is blocked at the lesion while conduction distal to it is preserved, because the axon is intact [r1].
If the force is greater or lasts longer, axons are disrupted, and the part of the axon beyond the lesion degenerates (Wallerian degeneration) [r9,r1].
The muscle supplied by the nerve loses its input and starts to waste; the sensory territory goes numb or tingly [r10].
Axons regrow from the injury site at about 1 mm a day if the pathway is intact; if the nerve is divided or the gap is large, repair is needed [r11,r12].

variants.name: Compression and entrapment in a tunnel
variants.description: Sustained pressure from a retinaculum, bone or oedema in a fibro-osseous tunnel (for example carpal, cubital or tarsal tunnel). Mild forms are neurapraxic; chronic or severe forms damage axons.

variants.name: Traction or stretch injury
variants.description: A joint forced beyond its range. The common peroneal nerve is highly vulnerable to stretch during varus stress, especially in posterolateral corner injuries [r7]. Traction to the brachial plexus is one of the devastating forms [r8].

variants.name: Crush and direct blow
variants.description: A blow over a superficial nerve (for example the fibular neck) squeezes the nerve against bone and may cause a neurapraxia or axonal injury [r1].

variants.name: Laceration or penetrating injury
variants.description: Cuts and penetrating wounds can partly or completely divide the nerve. Complete transection (neurotmesis) usually requires surgical repair [r2,r1].

variants.name: Ischaemic injury
variants.description: Reduced blood supply to the nerve, for example in compartment syndrome or a prolonged tourniquet, can cause conduction block or axonal loss [r1].

anatomy.text: A peripheral nerve is a bundle of axons, each wrapped by Schwann cells (myelin in myelinated fibres), grouped into fascicles by connective tissue layers: endoneurium around fibres, perineurium around fascicles and epineurium around the whole nerve (standard anatomy). A blood supply (vasa nervorum) runs along and into the nerve. Some nerves run through fibro-osseous tunnels, where retinacula, bone and tendons leave little spare room, and others lie close to bone, such as the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck [r7]. After injury, Schwann cells and macrophages clear the degenerating axon and support regrowth (standard teaching). The motor axons end at neuromuscular junctions, and muscle that loses input for a long time atrophies [r10,r13].

structures.name: Axon and Schwann cell (myelin sheath)
structures.role: Carry the electrical signal; Schwann cells support repair and regrowth after injury (standard teaching)

structures.name: Endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium
structures.role: Connective tissue layers that organise fibres into fascicles and form the 'tubes' along which axons regrow; Sunderland's degrees reflect how many layers are disrupted [r3,r2]

structures.name: Vasa nervorum
structures.role: The blood supply to the nerve; compression and stretch reduce it, causing ischaemic conduction block (mechanistic model)

structures.name: Fibro-osseous tunnel and retinaculum
structures.role: Confine the nerve; limited room makes it vulnerable to pressure from swelling, bone or retinaculum (anatomical reasoning)

structures.name: Target muscle and neuromuscular junction
structures.role: Motor endplates receive regrowing axons; muscle that stays denervated atrophies and limits reinnervation [r13,r10]

structures.name: Adjacent bone and ligaments
structures.role: Stretch or compress the nerve when forced out of position, as at the knee [r7]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In neurapraxia the lesion is a local conduction block: compound muscle and nerve action potentials on stimulating distal to the lesion are maintained, while stimulation above the lesion shows partial or complete conduction block [r1]. The axon is intact, so there is no Wallerian degeneration and, in the Seddon framework, recovery is presumed to be complete within 8 to 12 weeks, whereas axonotmesis is likely to leave sequelae (this statement was made in a facial nerve series) [r14]. In axonotmesis the axon is disrupted and the part distal to the lesion degenerates, a rapid, axon-autonomous process after axotomy known as Wallerian degeneration [r9]. In rat studies Wallerian degeneration occurs within days, denervated muscle atrophies within weeks, and regrowing axons advance at about 1 mm a day [r11]. In neurotmesis the nerve is completely divided and usually needs surgical repair [r2].

Time matters because muscle that stays denervated for a long time atrophies and loses its ability to be reinnervated. In a mouse nerve-graft model, recovery was worst in the group grafted 4 weeks after injury, and the 2-week group resembled the acute group [r13]. In humans, proximal injuries are problematic because the long distance makes it difficult to reinnervate distal muscles before irreversible changes occur [r1]. A divided nerve with a gap under 1 cm can often be repaired end to end after mobilisation, and a gap over 1 cm is treated with autologous nerve grafting, which remains the gold standard [r12]. Even with good surgery, functional recovery is often incomplete [r4].

structures.name: Axon
structures.effect: Intact in neurapraxia; disrupted in axonotmesis and neurotmesis, with Wallerian degeneration distally [r1,r9]

structures.name: Myelin and conduction
structures.effect: Focal conduction block at the lesion with preserved conduction distally in neurapraxia [r1]

structures.name: Connective tissue layers
structures.effect: Preserved in lesser injuries, which supports regrowth; disrupted in the severe Sunderland degrees and in neurotmesis, where the nerve may be divided and need repair [r3,r2]

structures.name: Vasa nervorum
structures.effect: Compression, stretch and ischaemia compromise blood flow to the nerve [r1]

muscles.name: Denervated muscle
muscles.effect: Progressive atrophy, which limits later reinnervation of motor endplates [r13,r10].

muscles.name: Antagonists and uninjured synergists
muscles.effect: Unopposed pull and altered movement patterns can lead to contracture and compensation (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Reinnervating muscle
muscles.effect: Regaining voluntary contraction as axons arrive, first in muscles nearest the injury; the process is slow and often incomplete [r4,r11].

cellular.description: Focal conduction block in neurapraxia; axons disrupted in axonotmesis and neurotmesis [r1].
The axon beyond the lesion degenerates by an axon-autonomous program [r9], and Schwann cells and macrophages clear the debris (standard teaching); in rats this occurs within days [r11].
Denervated muscle atrophies within weeks in rat studies [r11].

cellular.timing: Months at about 1 mm per day
cellular.description: Regrowing axons advance at about 1 mm a day [r11,r15]; in a 3-year-old with a repaired high radial nerve, wrist extension returned at 2.5 months and finger extension at 4 months, which was faster than the conventional rate [r15].
Reinnervated muscle and sensory fields mature; recovery is often incomplete, particularly after proximal injuries [r4,r1].

systems.effect: After injury there are changes at the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia that can limit regeneration and contribute to neuropathic pain [r10].
Weakness, atrophy, joint stiffness and contracture of the denervated segment, with altered gait or hand function [r10].
Ischaemia is a cause of nerve injury, and associated vascular injury should be considered in major trauma [r1].
Long recovery, uncertain outcome and loss of function affect well-being, work and sport; open discussion of realistic expectations helps [r8].
Macrophages and Schwann cells clear debris and support regrowth (standard teaching).

grading.system: Seddon classification (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis) and Sunderland classification (degrees I–V)

grades.description: Focal conduction block with the axon intact; conduction distal to the lesion is preserved and there is no Wallerian degeneration [r1,r2].
grades.prognosis: Presumed to recover completely, typically within 8 to 12 weeks (stated in a facial nerve series) [r14]

grades.description: Axon disrupted with Wallerian degeneration distally; the endoneurium and the other supporting layers are preserved (classical description of the degrees; Sunderland's paper has no abstract in PubMed) [r3,r2].
grades.prognosis: Regrowth along intact endoneurial tubes at about 1 mm a day with a good prospect of recovery, depending on distance (classical description) [r11]

grades.description: Axon and endoneurium disrupted within the fascicle, with intrafascicular scarring and misdirection of regrowing axons (classical description) [r3].
grades.prognosis: Variable and incomplete recovery; serial examination and electrodiagnosis guide decisions [r1]

grades.description: Axon, endoneurium and perineurium disrupted, with only the epineurium maintaining continuity: a neuroma-in-continuity (classical description) [r3].
grades.prognosis: Poor without surgery; exploration, often with intraoperative nerve action potential recording, guides repair [r1]

grades.description: Complete transection of the nerve; the stumps are separated and often need surgical repair [r2].
grades.prognosis: No useful recovery without surgery. A gap under 1 cm can be repaired end to end after mobilisation; a larger gap needs grafting [r12]

timeframes.summary: Time depends on the grade and on the distance from the lesion to the target muscle. Neurapraxia is presumed to recover within 8 to 12 weeks [r14]. After axonal injury, regrowth is about 1 mm a day [r11], so a muscle 300 mm below the lesion needs about 300 days for axons to arrive (arithmetic from the 1 mm a day rate), and function lags behind that. Denervated muscle atrophies over weeks, which is why proximal injuries are time-critical [r11,r1].

healing.phase: Injury and conduction block / Wallerian degeneration
healing.description: Wallerian degeneration of the axon beyond the lesion occurs within days in rat studies [r11]; early electrodiagnostic data can be informative in the first week [r1]
Presumed complete recovery within 8 to 12 weeks if the lesion is neurapraxia [r14]
Rate-limited by distance; typical timing depends on the injury level (clinical convention) [r11,r15]
Muscles regain voluntary contraction in sequence; rehabilitation builds strength and function (clinical convention) [r4]

milestones.label: Electrodiagnostic study informative
milestones.note: A great deal of important information can be obtained in the first week, though conventional teaching delays testing to about 3 weeks [r1]

milestones.label: Conventional timing of the first electrodiagnostic study
Review for referral if no recovery
milestones.note: About 3 months: a common clinical convention; proximal injuries need earlier decisions [r1]

milestones.label: Wrist and finger extension return after repair of a high radial nerve injury (one child)
milestones.note: Wrist dorsiflexion at 2.5 months and finger and thumb extension at 4 months [r15]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, not time-based. Return depends on the grade of injury, the muscles involved and the quality of reinnervation, and may take many months or never be complete. Protect the limb against re-injury and against overstretch, and return only when strength, sensation and control support the demands of the sport [r4,r1].

symptoms: Numbness, tingling or burning in the territory of one nerve, after a blow, stretch, compression or wound [r1]
Weakness, clumsiness or loss of function of the muscles it supplies (for example foot drop after common peroneal nerve injury) [r7]
Neuropathic pain, sometimes with sensitivity to touch (clinical convention)
In neurapraxia, symptoms that settle over weeks; in axonotmesis or neurotmesis, persistent loss that improves slowly or not at all [r14,r4]
Delayed signs such as muscle wasting, joint stiffness or skin changes in the denervated area (clinical convention)
signs: A sensory deficit that follows a nerve's territory, with reduced light touch, pinprick or two-point discrimination (clinical convention)
Motor weakness graded on the MRC scale (0–5) in the muscles of the nerve, with reduced reflexes in some (clinical convention)
Muscle wasting over weeks in the denervated muscles [r11]
Tinel's sign at the injury site, which advances distally as axons regrow (clinical convention)
Autonomic changes (dry skin, absent sweating) in a complete lesion (clinical convention)

subjective: Mechanism: penetrating injury, crush, stretch or ischaemia, and associated fractures, dislocations or ligament injuries [r1,r7]
Time of onset and course: immediate or delayed deficit, getting better, static or worse
Symptoms: numbness, tingling, weakness, pain and function lost; hand dominance, work and sport
Associated injuries and care so far: reduced fracture or dislocation, casts, splints, surgery, wounds
Medical history: diabetes, alcohol, previous neuropathy, medication and anticoagulants (clinical reasoning)
Expectations and goals; mood and sleep, because recovery is long [r8]
observation: Wounds, bruising and swelling over the course of the nerve, and limb posture (for example wrist drop or foot drop)
Muscle bulk compared with the other side, and skin changes in the territory
Gait (foot drop, steppage), grip and hand function [r7]
palpation: Palpation along the nerve for tenderness and Tinel's sign at the site of injury; mark the most distal point of Tinel's sign and repeat over time (clinical convention)
Tight tunnels or retinacula, oedema or a haematoma that may compress the nerve
Compartments, if there is a fracture or severe swelling (clinical convention)
rangeOfMotion: Passive range of the joints supplied by the nerve, to detect contracture (clinical convention)
Active range, which is limited by weakness
strength: Grade each muscle of the nerve on the MRC 0–5 scale and record all muscles and the pattern, because an incomplete pattern suggests a partial lesion (clinical convention)
Test the nearest uninjured nerves to localise the level and exclude a proximal lesion (clinical convention)
Grip dynamometry or hand-held dynamometry for serial tracking
neuro: Map sensory loss to a nerve's territory with light touch, pinprick and two-point discrimination, and distinguish nerve territory from dermatome (clinical convention)
Reflexes and sympathetic signs (skin temperature, sweating) (clinical convention)
Re-test at each visit and record the progress of Tinel's sign: the clinical signs of regrowth guide referral [r1]
functional: Gait, heel walk and toe walk (foot drop), hand function tasks and grip
Ability to perform sport-specific tasks, noting compensation
Safety: protective sensation, falls risk and skin protection in the numb area (clinical reasoning)

specialTests.name: Tinel's sign (percussion along the nerve)
specialTests.purpose: Locate the site of injury and track regrowth
specialTests.procedure: Tap lightly along the nerve from distal to proximal and note the most distal point that reproduces tingling in the sensory territory.
specialTests.positive: Tingling in the nerve's territory on percussion; a point that moves distally over weeks suggests regrowth. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: MRC manual muscle testing of each muscle
specialTests.purpose: Grade motor loss and track reinnervation in a pattern
specialTests.procedure: Grade each muscle supplied by the nerve from 0 (no contraction) to 5 (normal) against gravity and resistance.
specialTests.positive: A defined pattern of weakness in a nerve's muscles; improvement in a proximal-to-distal sequence suggests reinnervation. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Sensory mapping and two-point discrimination
specialTests.purpose: Define the territory and severity of sensory loss
specialTests.procedure: Map light touch and pinprick on the skin, and compare with the other side; use two-point discrimination for finger pulps.
specialTests.positive: Loss in the territory of a single nerve, with return from the edges inward as the nerve recovers. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Nerve provocation (neurodynamic) test
specialTests.purpose: Assess neural tension in entrapment, not in acute traction injuries
specialTests.procedure: Place the limb in the nerve's tensioning position and note reproduction of symptoms; avoid forcing it in an acute, repaired or severely injured nerve.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the familiar tingling or pain. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed and the test should not be used to stretch an injured nerve.

clinicalRules.name: Seddon and Sunderland grading
clinicalRules.description: A framework for prognosis: neurapraxia is a conduction block with the axon intact and is presumed to recover completely within 8 to 12 weeks, whereas axonotmesis is likely to leave sequelae [r14,r2,r1]. Electrodiagnosis helps to classify the injury, localise it and quantify axon loss [r6].

clinicalRules.name: No validated clinical decision rule for referral
clinicalRules.description: Decisions about exploration depend on the injury, its level and the time since injury, and need serial clinical and electrodiagnostic examination; proximal injuries need earlier decisions [r1,r7].

outcomeMeasures.name: MRC muscle grade for each muscle (0–5)
outcomeMeasures.use: Tracks reinnervation and recovery of strength (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Sensory testing (light touch, pinprick, two-point discrimination)
outcomeMeasures.use: Tracks sensory recovery; sensory, motor and grip strength outcomes were used in a trial of median nerve repair [r16]

outcomeMeasures.name: Grip or hand-held dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective strength tracking over months; grip strength was measured in a median nerve repair trial [r16]

outcomeMeasures.name: Advancing Tinel's sign (distance in mm)
outcomeMeasures.use: Clinical marker of axonal regrowth, mapped at each visit (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Electrodiagnostic findings (nerve conduction and EMG)
outcomeMeasures.use: Localise, grade and monitor the injury; the optimal timing depends on the clinical question [r1,r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-reported function and pain scales for the limb
outcomeMeasures.use: Capture disability and neuropathic pain (clinical convention)

imaging.modality: Electrodiagnostic study (nerve conduction studies and needle EMG)
imaging.indication: Any suspected nerve injury where localising and grading would change management
imaging.findings: In neurapraxia, conduction distal to the lesion is maintained and a conduction block is found above it; in axonotmesis and neurotmesis the picture depends on the time since injury; useful information can be obtained in the first week, with conventional testing at about 3 weeks [r1,r6]

imaging.indication: To show nerve continuity, a neuroma or entrapment, and to guide intervention
imaging.findings: High-frequency ultrasound and electrodiagnostic studies were used together to confirm a radial nerve injury in a case report [r15]

imaging.indication: Deep or proximal injuries, brachial plexus injuries and surgical planning
imaging.findings: Imaging review contributes to the diagnosis of brachial plexus injury alongside history, examination and electrodiagnostic studies [r8]

imaging.indication: Fractures or dislocations that accompany or cause the nerve injury, such as knee dislocation with CPN palsy

differentials.name: Common peroneal nerve injury
differentials.distinguishing: Foot drop and dorsal foot numbness after a blow or varus injury at the fibular neck; the commonest peripheral nerve injury in multiligament knee trauma [r7].

differentials.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual median nerve compression at the wrist with night symptoms and thenar weakness; a chronic entrapment, usually neurapraxic early.

differentials.name: Cubital tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow, with ring and little finger numbness and intrinsic weakness.

differentials.name: Stinger or burner (brachial plexus traction)
differentials.distinguishing: Transient burning arm pain and weakness after a shoulder depression or neck lateral flexion injury in contact sport; usually a brief neurapraxia, with persistent deficit needing review (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Acute compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Pain out of proportion, a tense compartment and neurological change after trauma or exertion; a surgical emergency that can itself injure nerves [r1].

differentials.name: Cervical or lumbar radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Dermatomal or myotomal pattern with neck or back pain and a positive root tension test, rather than a single peripheral nerve territory (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Complex regional pain syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Disproportionate pain, allodynia, swelling and autonomic and trophic change after an injury, beyond a nerve territory (clinical convention).

redFlags: Open wound over a nerve with new motor or sensory loss, or a penetrating injury: suspect laceration or transection and arrange urgent surgical assessment; decisions about exploration need to be made quickly [r1].
Expanding haematoma, cold or pulseless limb, or severe pain with a tense compartment after trauma: suspect vascular injury or acute compartment syndrome and send to emergency [r1].
Knee dislocation or multiligament injury with foot drop: arrange urgent medical review, because the common peroneal nerve is involved in 16% to 40% and the prognosis is poor [r7].

Progressive weakness or numbness, or no clinical or electrical sign of recovery by about 3 months: refer to a peripheral nerve surgeon or neurologist without delay; proximal injuries need earlier decisions [r1,r13].
Brachial plexus injury or a high-energy shoulder, neck or upper limb injury with weakness: refer early to a multidisciplinary team with a peripheral nerve surgeon [r8].
Bilateral signs, bladder or bowel change, saddle numbness or upper motor neuron signs: suspect a central or spinal cause and arrange emergency assessment (clinical convention).

management.principles: Management starts with careful, repeated clinical examination and, where it changes management, early electrodiagnosis [r1]. Management is determined by the severity and location of the injury, the timing of presentation, associated injuries and serial clinical and electrodiagnostic results [r7]. Neurapraxia is expected to recover without surgery, whereas a divided nerve needs repair, and the time to surgery matters because muscle that stays denervated atrophies [r14,r13,r12]. Rehabilitation protects the limb, maintains joint range and muscle health, and re-educates sensation and function while axons regrow at about 1 mm a day [r11,r8]. Evidence for exercise and electrical stimulation to promote regeneration is mostly preclinical, and there is too little human research to reach firm conclusions [r5]. Care is best delivered by a multidisciplinary team [r8].

medical.name: Observation with serial clinical and electrodiagnostic review
medical.description: For suspected neurapraxia or incomplete lesions, serial examination and electrodiagnostic studies, with the timing of testing chosen for the clinical question [r1,r7].

medical.name: Surgical exploration and repair (neurolysis, end-to-end repair, grafting)
medical.description: End-to-end neurorrhaphy is the gold standard for a sectioned nerve; a gap under 1 cm can be closed after mobilisation, and a gap over 1 cm is bridged with an autologous nerve graft [r12]. Surgical options include neurolysis, primary repair, intercalary grafting, tendon transfer and nerve transfer [r7]. Exploration with intraoperative nerve action potential recording often guides the choice [r1].

medical.name: Nerve transfer or tendon transfer for proximal or late injuries
medical.description: When reinnervation of distal muscles is unlikely in time, nerve or tendon transfers restore function; limited evidence supports early one-stage nerve reconstruction with tendon transfer in common peroneal injuries [r7,r8].

medical.name: Earlier decision-making for proximal injuries
medical.description: Proximal nerve injuries are problematic because the long distance makes it difficult to reinnervate distal muscles before irreversible changes occur, so decisions about exploration must be made more quickly [r1]. In a mouse model recovery was worst after a 4-week delay before grafting [r13].

medical.name: Analgesia for neuropathic pain
medical.description: Neuropathic pain after nerve injury may need medical management with a doctor or pain service. No trial evidence was found in the sources reviewed.

medical.name: Multidisciplinary care
medical.description: Care of complex injuries such as brachial plexus injuries involves peripheral nerve surgeons, neurology, hand therapy, physiotherapy, pain management, social work and mental health [r8].

physio.name: Education, baseline documentation and serial re-testing
physio.description: Explain the grades, the slow rate of regrowth (about 1 mm a day) and the need for follow-up; record a baseline of MRC grades, sensory map and Tinel's point, and repeat to detect recovery or stalling [r1,r11].

physio.name: Protection, positioning and orthosis
physio.description: Non-surgical options include orthosis wear and physical therapy, for example an ankle-foot orthosis for foot drop [r7]. Protect numb skin and avoid sustained compression or stretch.

physio.name: Maintain joint range and prevent contracture
physio.description: Active and passive range of motion of the affected joints within surgical restrictions, to prevent stiffness while muscles are weak (clinical practice).

physio.name: Graded active exercise during regeneration
physio.description: A systematic review of 60 mostly preclinical studies found that an early physical program with active exercise and/or electrical stimulation promotes axonal regenerative responses and prevents maladaptive responses, but some detrimental effects of exercising and stimulating too early after nerve repair were recorded, and human research is too limited for firm conclusions [r5]. Use low-load, pain-free, surgeon-approved exercise.

physio.name: Electrical stimulation (percutaneous or transcutaneous)
physio.description: In a randomised trial of 23 patients after median nerve repair, percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation added to conventional rehabilitation gave greater improvement in sensory function, motor function and grip strength than transcutaneous stimulation added to conventional rehabilitation [r16]. Reviews report that electrical stimulation may promote axon regeneration and reduce muscle atrophy, but standardised protocols are lacking [r10,r17].

physio.name: Other physical agents (therapeutic ultrasound, photobiomodulation)
physio.description: Ultrasound and photobiomodulation are discussed in a recent review as modalities that may support nerve regeneration, but standardised treatment protocols and long-term effectiveness are lacking [r17].

physio.name: Sensory re-education, desensitisation and functional retraining
physio.description: Graded sensory and task-specific training as sensation returns; hand therapy and physiotherapy are part of multidisciplinary care [r8].

physio.name: Stretching or forcing the injured or repaired nerve
physio.description: Stretch is a mechanism of nerve injury [r1]; do not tension an injured or recently repaired nerve, and respect surgical precautions (clinical reasoning).

physio.name: Heavy resistance or vigorous stimulation too early after repair
physio.description: Some detrimental effects of exercising and electrical stimulation too early after nerve repair were recorded in preclinical studies [r5].

physio.name: Prolonged watchful waiting without reassessment
physio.description: Denervated muscle atrophies and recovery worsens with the time before repair in a mouse model, so a lack of recovery should prompt referral, not simply more time [r13,r1].

education: Nerves heal slowly. Regrowth is about a millimetre a day, so recovery is measured in months, and the distance from the injury to the muscle matters.
Mild injuries (neurapraxia) usually recover within weeks to a few months. More severe injuries can need surgery.
Protect numb skin from burns, cuts and pressure, and avoid positions that squeeze or stretch the nerve.
Keep the joints moving and the other muscles strong while the nerve recovers.
Tell us if strength or sensation stops improving, because earlier referral gives surgery the best chance.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation follows the medical plan and the type of injury, and is criteria-based because reinnervation is slow and variable. The stages are: protect and maintain; support the reinnervation phase; strengthen as muscles recover; and return to function and sport. Time frames are only guides: regrowth is about 1 mm a day [r11], so distance sets the timeline. Evidence for exercise and electrical stimulation during regeneration is mostly preclinical, so exercise is graded, low load and agreed with the surgeon [r5]. Doses below are common clinical conventions, not trial-based prescriptions.

stages.name: Protect & maintain
stages.timeframe: Early weeks (until recovery signs or after surgery per the surgeon)
goals: Protect the nerve and denervated skin
Maintain joint range and prevent contracture
precautions: Follow surgical restrictions after repair and avoid stretching an injured or repaired nerve [r1]
Do not use heavy resistance or vigorous stimulation too early after repair [r5]
Protect numb skin from heat, cold and pressure

exercises.name: Active range of motion of the unaffected joints
exercises.cues: Keep the rest of the limb moving; no pain

exercises.name: Passive or active-assisted range of the affected joint (for example ankle)
exercises.dosage: 2 × 10 each direction, 2–3 times a day, within surgical limits
exercises.cues: Gentle, slow movement; prevent stiffness, never force

exercises.name: Heel slide (knee and hip range)
exercises.cues: Smooth and comfortable range

exercises.name: Cardiovascular fitness that spares the injured limb
exercises.cues: Choose exercise that avoids pressure on the nerve

exercises.name: Orthosis fitting and skin protection routine
exercises.cues: Use the orthosis to prevent foot drop or wrist drop contracture and to protect the skin [r7]

progressionCriteria: Wound healed and surgical restrictions lifted (if applicable)
Joint range maintained within about 10% of the other side (clinical convention)
Baseline MRC grades, sensory map and Tinel's point documented

stages.name: Support reinnervation
goals: Support the muscle while axons regrow
Track the advancing Tinel's sign and early contraction
Begin sensory re-education as sensation returns
precautions: Refer if no clinical or electrical recovery by about 3 months, or sooner for proximal injuries [r1]

exercises.name: Gentle isometric or low-load active contractions of the reinnervating muscle once any contraction appears
exercises.dosage: 5–10 contractions of 3–5 s, 2–3 times a day, stop before fatigue
exercises.cues: Think about the movement; short, high-quality contractions

exercises.name: Neuromuscular or electrical stimulation if available and cleared
exercises.dosage: Per clinic protocol and surgeon approval
exercises.cues: Evidence is limited and protocols are not standardised [r10,r17]

exercises.name: Glute bridge (proximal strength)
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels

exercises.name: Single-leg balance (lower limb)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 20–30 s each side, daily, with support if needed
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level; use the orthosis if prescribed

exercises.name: Sensory re-education and desensitisation
exercises.cues: Graded textures and tasks as sensation returns

progressionCriteria: Visible or palpable contraction in the target muscle (MRC 1 or above)
Tinel's sign advancing distally at a steady pace
No increase in pain after exercise

stages.name: Strengthen as muscles recover
goals: Progress strength as the MRC grade rises
Wean the orthosis as strength allows
Prepare for return to work and sport
precautions: Load increases only if there is no pain, swelling or fatigue-related loss of control the next day
Review progress with the surgeon or neurologist if recovery stalls [r1]

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise
exercises.cues: Even weight through both feet

exercises.name: Bodyweight squat
exercises.cues: Whole foot down, knees tracking over the toes

exercises.name: Step-up
exercises.cues: Control the pelvis and the foot

exercises.name: Wrist extension (upper limb injuries)
exercises.cues: Forearm supported; only if the nerve has recovered enough

exercises.name: Grip strengthening (upper limb)
exercises.cues: Smooth squeeze and release

exercises.name: Neural glide (sciatic or median nerve) once cleared
exercises.dosage: 2 × 8–10, daily, pain-free, only once cleared by the surgeon
exercises.cues: Gentle sliding; never a stretch into tingling

progressionCriteria: MRC grade 4 or above in the key muscles (clinical convention)
Normal gait without an orthosis, or with minimal support
Sensation returning to protective level or better

stages.name: Return to function & sport
goals: Return to work and sport-specific tasks
Protect against re-injury and long-term skin damage
precautions: Return only when strength, sensation and control support the sport and with surgeon approval
Continue protecting areas with reduced sensation
Accept that recovery may be incomplete and plan modifications [r4]

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place, then forward
exercises.cues: Soft landing; stick it for 2 s

exercises.name: Jump and soft landing
exercises.cues: Hips and knees bent on landing

exercises.name: Change-of-direction drills
exercises.dosage: 2 sessions a week, planned then reactive
exercises.cues: Land under control, knee over the foot

exercises.name: Sport-specific skill and contact progression
exercises.cues: Monitor sensation, strength and fatigue

exercises.name: Strength maintenance (hip, calf, hand)
exercises.cues: Controlled tempo, steady progression

progressionCriteria: Strength near the other side (about 90%) on dynamometry (clinical convention)
Sport-specific tests completed without compensation or loss of control
Protective sensation adequate for the sport
Surgeon, athlete and clinicians agree on return

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria exist for peripheral nerve injury; the criteria below are clinical conventions and depend on the grade, the nerve and the sport
Evidence of reinnervation of the key muscles (MRC grade 4 or above) and adequate sensation, including protective sensation (clinical convention)
Strength near the other side (about 90%) and normal functional movement without an orthosis, or with an orthosis suited to the sport
Completion of graded sport-specific loading with no pain, tingling or loss of control after sessions
Surgeon or neurologist approval and a plan to monitor skin, sensation and strength
Realistic expectations, as recovery may be incomplete, particularly after proximal injuries or Sunderland III–V lesions [r4,r1]
tests: MRC manual muscle testing of key muscles
Dynamometry compared with the other side (grip or hand-held)
Sensory testing (light touch, pinprick, two-point discrimination)
Repeat electrodiagnostic study if recovery is unclear [r1,r6]

prognosis: Prognosis depends on the grade of injury, the nerve, the level and the time to repair. Neurapraxia is presumed to recover completely, typically within 8 to 12 weeks, whereas axonotmesis is likely to leave sequelae [r14]. Axons regrow at about 1 mm a day, so proximal injuries are difficult to reinnervate before irreversible changes occur in muscle [r11,r1]. Reliable treatments that guarantee full functional recovery are scarce [r4]. Common peroneal nerve injuries have a poor prognosis compared with other peripheral nerve injuries [r7], and complex brachial plexus injuries can have life-altering effects, although comprehensive multidisciplinary care and realistic goals can give meaningful recovery [r8]. Functional recovery worsens with increasing denervation time before repair in a mouse model [r13]. Surgery can restore useful function in many divided nerves, depending on gap length, graft quality and timing [r12]. Neuropathic pain and sensory loss may persist [r10].
prevention: Avoid sustained pressure and extreme positions over superficial nerves, such as the fibular neck and the ulnar nerve at the elbow, and pad and check casts, splints and straps (clinical reasoning).
Protect against high-risk movements and contacts, such as severe varus stress at the knee, through appropriate protection and conditioning in contact sport [r7].
Recognise and treat compartment syndrome and fractures quickly to prevent secondary nerve injury [r1].
After any significant limb trauma, record a baseline neurological examination so that new deficits are not missed (clinical practice).
Do not tension an injured or recently repaired nerve, and follow surgical precautions during rehabilitation [r1].
Refer early when the nerve does not recover, because the time to repair affects outcome [r13,r1].
clinicalPearls: Document everything at baseline: motor grades, sensory map and the most distal point of Tinel's sign. Recovery and stalling are only visible if you have a baseline [r1].
Think in axonal distances. At about 1 mm a day, a muscle 300 mm below the lesion is 300 days away, so proximal injuries need earlier decisions [r11,r1].
Neurapraxia is the reassuring diagnosis: the axon is intact and conduction distal to the lesion is preserved. Expect improvement within 8 to 12 weeks, and think again if it does not arrive [r1,r14].
Electrodiagnostic testing is not only for week 3: useful information can be obtained in the first week, and the best timing depends on the clinical question [r1].

Exercise and electrical stimulation are promising in preclinical work, but too little is known in humans and too-early or too-heavy loading after repair may be harmful. Keep loading low and agreed with the surgeon [r5].
The common peroneal nerve is injured in 16% to 40% of multiligament knee injuries. Test dorsiflexion, great toe extension and dorsal foot sensation after any severe knee injury [r7].

animation.title: How a peripheral nerve is injured and recovers

captions.text: An athlete changes direction at speed in a contact sport.
A blow or a fall drives the outer side of the knee into the ground.
The common peroneal nerve runs close under the skin around the fibular neck.
The nerve is squeezed against bone, and a severe twist can also stretch it.
The athlete has numbness over the foot and a weak ankle that drops.
Zooming into the nerve: shown as a nerve in a tight tunnel.

actions.text: Peripheral nerve in a fibro-osseous tunnel
Blood supply to the nerve is squeezed
Axons regrow about 1 mm a day

captions.text: The nerve runs through a tight tunnel beside bone and the retinaculum.
Pressure from a blow or swelling squeezes the nerve in the tunnel.
The small blood vessels that feed the nerve are compressed too, so the nerve loses oxygen.
The nerve fires abnormally: tingling and numbness, then a conduction block. This is neurapraxia.
With greater force or a longer time, axons are damaged: axonotmesis.
The muscle that the nerve supplies loses its input and starts to waste.
If the pathway is intact, axons regrow from the injury at about 1 mm a day.
Healthy nerve: myelinated axons carry signals, fed by small blood vessels.
Compression: pressure on the nerve starts to block the signal.
Ischaemia: the blood supply to the nerve is reduced, so conduction fails.
Demyelination: the myelin is damaged at the lesion. The axon is intact, so recovery is expected.
Axonal injury: with greater force or time, the axon itself is disrupted.
Wallerian degeneration: the axon beyond the lesion breaks down and is cleared.
Regeneration: axons regrow along the pathway at about 1 mm a day, so recovery takes months.
